messages.subject: Scantwo results interpretation
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I ran both scanone and scantwo analaysis to explore and identify the QTLs linked to my trait. Using the scanone I got three QTL on chr 3, 4 and 5. Then, I tried the CIM analysis to see if I could find other QTLs while controling for the ones that were already identified and no further QTL was found. However, I was a bit troubled after running a scantwo analysis and now I am not sure If I am interpreting that well.

Here the results of the scantwo :

> summary(out17,perms=operm17,alphas=c(0.05,0.05,0,0.05,0.05),pvalues=TRUE)
 pos1f pos2f lod.full pval lod.fv1 pval lod.int <http://lod.int> pval
c3:c4 20.2 40.4 9.30 0 4.63 0.020 0.5676 1
c3:c5 20.2 10.0 10.02 0 4.76 0.015 0.1099 1
c4:c5 14.2 10.0 8.82 0 3.56 0.135 0.0124 1
pos1a pos2a lod.add pval lod.av1 pval
c3:c4 20.2 25.6 8.73 0 4.07 0.000
c3:c5 20.2 10.0 9.91 0 4.65 0.000
c4:c5 14.2 10.0 8.81 0 3.55 0.002

So here is what I understand from the R/qtl guide, I would like to make sure that understood well so tell me if I am wrong :

The locations for the QTLs on chr 3 and 5 are the same no matter if we consider the pos of the full model posf or of the additive model posa, is that right ?
But with the lines in green it seems that there are two QTLs on chr 4 that are not located at the same place right ? One is at 40.4 cM for posf / 25.6 cM for posa (first line) and the other one is at 14.2cM for both posf and posa. So the fact that I have two lines with chr 4 with different locations means that I might have two QTLs there ? With only additive effect as the lod.int <http://lod.int> is very small ?

Compared to scanone and using CIM, both QTLs on 3 and 5 were found at the same location but the QTL on chr 4 identified with scanone was located at 14.2cM when B3 was used as covariate and 25.6cM with B3 and B5 as covariates.

The shape of the courbe could suggest the existence of QTLs on the location 14, 25 and 40cM as we can see high peaks at these locations for the SIM that is why I ran the scantwo to see which QTLs were really detected.

Thank you all for your help !

messages.subject: Re: Scantwo results interpretation
messages.body_plain:
With no evidence for interactions, I'd focus on the estimated positions with additive QTL.
chr 3 at 20.2, chr 5 at 10.0, and chr 4 at 14.2-25.6.

The locus on chr 4 moves to position 40.4 when you include an interaction with the chr 3 QTL, but since there's no evidence for an interaction, I would just ignore that.

I'd use makeqtl(), fitqtl(), and refineqtl(), to bring the three QTL together into a single model. You can use addqtl() to scan for an additional QTL, for example to see whether there is evidence for an additional QTL on chr 4.

karl

Thanks,
Josh

Is this ambiguity irrelevant in this particular case, or is it important that whatever phasing solution I come up be able to explicitly record which homologous chromosome in the parents each progeny genotype came from?

Hopefully this makes sense & thanks so much for any advice you can provide!
Scott

messages.body_plain:
Markers segregating like ABxBB (where the female parent is heterozygous) will be about half with the A on one chromosome and half where it's on the other chromosome. Phasing the genotypes identifies those two groups.
Having done that, think of the cross as ABxCD, and the markers as either ABxBB or BAxBB. In each case the progeny are going to be either AB or BB.

ABxBB:
    AB progeny = AC or AD = A = 5
    BB progeny = BC or BD = B = 6

BAxBB: swap the 5's and 6's
    AB progeny = BC or BD = B = 6
    BB progeny = AC or AD = A = 5

If instead the male parent is heterozygous, we'd have

BBxAB:
    AB progeny = AC or BC = C = 7
    BB progeny = AD or BD = D = 8

BBxBA:
    AB progeny = AD or BD = D = 8
    BB progeny = AC or BC = C = 7

karl

messages.body_plain:
I can't think of a simple way to do this.

You can use lodint() or bayesint() with expandtomarkers=TRUE to get a QTL interval; expandtomarkers=TRUE forces the end points to be at typed genetic markers.

    data(hyper)
    hyper <- calc.genoprob(hyper, step=1)
    out <- scanone(hyper, method="em")
    lodint(out, chr=4, expandtomarkers=TRUE)
    bayesint(out, chr=4, expandtomarkers=TRUE)

If you want to find all of the markers in the region of a QTL, you might convert the genetic map to a data frame, find the marker at the QTL position, and then show the surrounding markers.

    maxpos <- max(out)
    marker <- find.marker(hyper, maxpos$chr, maxpos$pos)
    map <- pull.map(hyper)
    map_df <- map2table(map)
    row_index <- which(rownames(map_df) == marker)
    map_df[row_index + (-3:3), ]

karl

It would be helpful if you provided an example to show exactly what you're looking at, but I take it you're looking at a 4-way cross. We treat that as the parents being AB x CD, so the offspring genotypes are AC, BC, AD, BD. The intercept is then the estimated average phenotype for the AC genotype, and the BC,AD,BD coefficients are for the differences between the average phenotype for these genotypes and the average phenotype for the AC genotype.

karl
